questions.title: Linear Search Index
questions.description:
The program scaffolding (input reading and main) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def linear_search(values, x):

Return the index of the FIRST occurrence of x in values (0-based), or -1 if x does not appear. A simple left-to-right scan is expected.

Input Format:
Line 1: n, the number of values.
Line 2: n integers.
Line 3: the target x.

Output Format:
One line with the index of the first occurrence of x, or -1.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 1000
-1000000 <= value <= 1000000
-1000000 <= x <= 1000000
questions.sourcecode:
import sys


def linear_search(values, x):
    for i in range(len(values)):
        if values[i] == x:
            return i
    return -1


data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
values = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
x = int(data[1 + n])
print(linear_search(values, x))

questions.title: Binary Search Index
questions.description:
The program scaffolding (input reading and main) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def binary_search(values, x):

values is sorted in ascending order. Return the index of x using binary search (0-based), or -1 if x does not appear.

Input Format:
Line 1: n, the number of values.
Line 2: n integers in ascending order.
Line 3: the target x.

Output Format:
One line with the index of x, or -1.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 1000
-1000000 <= value <= 1000000
-1000000 <= x <= 1000000
questions.sourcecode:
import sys


def binary_search(values, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(values) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if values[mid] == x:
            return mid
        if values[mid] < x:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1


data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
values = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
x = int(data[1 + n])
print(binary_search(values, x))

questions.title: Binary Search Probe Count
questions.description:
A storage profiler counts how many middle-element checks (probes) binary search performs, because every probe costs a disk read.

The program scaffolding (input reading and main) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def probe_count(values, x):

Run the standard binary search with mid = (lo + hi) // 2 and count how many times a middle element is examined until x is found. x is always present, so the loop ends on a match.

Input Format:
Line 1: n, the number of values.
Line 2: n integers in ascending order.
Line 3: the target x (always present).

Output Format:
One line with the number of probes.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 1000
-1000000 <= value <= 1000000
-1000000 <= x <= 1000000
questions.sourcecode:
import sys


def probe_count(values, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(values) - 1
    probes = 0
    while lo <= hi:
        probes += 1
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if values[mid] == x:
            break
        if values[mid] < x:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return probes


data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
values = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
x = int(data[1 + n])
print(probe_count(values, x))

questions.title: Closest Element to the Target
questions.description:
A thermostat scans a sorted calibration table for the temperature closest to the setpoint. If two elements are equally close, the smaller one (first in ascending order) wins. No min() shortcuts — track the best candidate yourself.

The program scaffolding (input reading and main) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def closest_element(values, x):

values is sorted ascending. Return the element of values minimizing the absolute difference to x; on a tie return the smaller element.

Input Format:
Line 1: n, the number of values.
Line 2: n integers in ascending order.
Line 3: the target x.

Output Format:
One line with the closest element.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 1000
-1000000 <= value <= 1000000
-1000000 <= x <= 1000000
questions.sourcecode:
import sys


def closest_element(values, x):
    best = values[0]
    bestd = values[0] - x
    if bestd < 0:
        bestd = -bestd
    i = 1
    while i < len(values):
        d = values[i] - x
        if d < 0:
            d = -d
        if d < bestd:
            bestd = d
            best = values[i]
        i += 1
    return best


data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
values = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
x = int(data[1 + n])
print(closest_element(values, x))

questions.title: Two Sum in a Sorted List
questions.description:
A payment matcher scans a sorted list of amounts for two entries summing to a target. The sorted order allows the two-pointer walk — both pointers start at the ends.

The program scaffolding (input reading and main) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def two_sum_pair(values, target):

values is sorted ascending and a pair summing to target always exists. Use the two-pointer walk (lo at the start, hi at the end; move lo right when the sum is too small, hi left when too large) and return the FIRST matching pair as (values[lo], values[hi]).

Input Format:
Line 1: n, the number of values.
Line 2: n integers in ascending order.
Line 3: the target sum.

Output Format:
One line with the two matched values, space-separated.

Constraints:
2 <= n <= 1000
-1000000 <= value <= 1000000
-2000000 <= target <= 2000000
questions.sourcecode:
import sys


def two_sum_pair(values, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(values) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        s = values[lo] + values[hi]
        if s == target:
            return values[lo], values[hi]
        if s < target:
            lo += 1
        else:
            hi -= 1
    return -1, -1


data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
values = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
target = int(data[1 + n])
a, b = two_sum_pair(values, target)
print(a, b)

questions.title: The Missing Number
questions.description:
A sensor gateway drops exactly one packet id per batch. Ids run from 0 to n and the batch holds n of them. Recover the missing id in one pass — sorting the batch is forbidden on the wire.

The program scaffolding (input reading and main) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def missing_number(batch):

batch holds n DISTINCT integers from the range 0..n (so exactly one value of 0..n is absent). Return the missing value. A single loop (xor or running arithmetic) is enough.

Input Format:
Line 1: n, the number of received ids.
Line 2: n distinct integers from 0..n.

Output Format:
One line with the missing id.

Constraints:
1 <= n <= 100000
batch values are distinct and taken from 0..n
questions.inputconstrains: 1 <= n <= 100000; batch holds n distinct values from 0..n
questions.sourcecode:
import sys


def missing_number(batch):
    n = len(batch)
    acc = 0
    i = 0
    while i <= n:
        acc ^= i
        i += 1
    i = 0
    while i < n:
        acc ^= batch[i]
        i += 1
    return acc


data = sys.stdin.read().split()
n = int(data[0])
batch = list(map(int, data[1:1 + n]))
print(missing_number(batch))

questions.title: Peak Element Index
questions.description:
A load monitor reads a sequence where the traffic rises then falls somewhere (no two neighbours are equal). Report the peak using the standard converging binary search.

The program scaffolding (input reading and main) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def peak_index(values):

A peak is an element strictly greater than its neighbours (boundary elements only need to beat their single neighbour). Run exactly this binary search and return the index it converges to: lo = 0, hi = n-1; while lo < hi: mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if values[mid] < values[mid + 1]: lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid; return lo. No two adjacent values are equal, so this always lands on a valid peak.

Input Format:
Line 1: n, the number of values (n >= 2).
Line 2: n integers, no two adjacent values equal.

Output Format:
One line with the peak index.

Constraints:
2 <= n <= 1000
-1000000 <= value <= 1000000

def peak_index(values):
    lo, hi = 0, len(values) - 1
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if values[mid] < values[mid + 1]:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo

questions.title: Integer Square Root by Search
questions.description:
An embedded device has no floating-point unit: square roots are computed by binary searching the answer space.

The program scaffolding (input reading and main) is already set up for you. Implement only this function:

    def integer_sqrt(x):

Return the largest integer r with r * r <= x, searching the range 1..x with your own binary search (multiply, never use pow or math.sqrt).

Input Format:
Line 1: the integer x (x >= 1).

Output Format:
One line with the floor of the square root of x.

Constraints:
1 <= x <= 1000000000
questions.sourcecode:
import sys


def integer_sqrt(x):
    lo, hi = 1, x
    ans = 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if mid * mid <= x:
            ans = mid
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return ans


x = int(sys.stdin.read().strip())
print(integer_sqrt(x))
